narrative:
Your application was rejected because the model predicted a 51.8% chance you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt, meaning it was slightly more confident you would not pass than that you would. Your LSAT score of 36 was also slightly below the average of 37.27 for successful students, though your undergraduate GPA of 3.40 was actually higher than their average of 3.24. In every single scenario, the only feature that changed was your undergraduate GPA, which decreased by an average of 0.2 points—from 3.40 to 3.20. This means the model sees your high GPA as a potential red flag, possibly because it contrasts sharply with your low law school deciles, suggesting your undergraduate success did not translate to law school performance. No other features—like your LSAT score, family income, or full-time status—ever changed, indicating they are less influential in the model's decision for your case.

The key insight is that the model considers your undergraduate GPA as the most impactful factor to adjust, but in a counterintuitive way: lowering it would make the prediction flip to "pass." This likely reflects a pattern where students with very high GPAs but low law school grades are seen as underperformers, while a more moderate GPA aligned with your law school standing would be more consistent. For you, this means focusing on improving your law school performance—specifically your Year 1 and Year 3 deciles—would be more realistic than changing your GPA. Since your deciles never changed in the counterfactuals, the model suggests that even small improvements in your law school grades could shift the prediction, but the current analysis highlights that your GPA is the lever the model uses to signal inconsistency. To realistically improve your chances, aim to raise your law school deciles closer to the average of 6, which would better align with your strong undergraduate record and reduce the model's concern about your bar exam readiness.
